selected.name: Formal/technical machinery calibrated to the question's apparent level
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the weight of formalism/machinery in the answer matches the apparent difficulty level signaled by the question. 10 = the level of technical apparatus (notation, cited theorems, generality) is well matched to what the question calls for -- neither overkill for a simple question nor underpowered for a hard one. 0 = a clear mismatch, such as heavy multi-step formal machinery deployed on a question that reads as elementary/homework-level, or a bare hand-wave on a question that clearly demands rigor.
selected.rationale: R03 answers an elementary sign-of-exponent question with a matched, compact algebraic demonstration and is dense_high_card_low; R56, by contrast, deploys a full 3x3 cofactor-matrix inverse and multi-equation derivation for what reads as a similarly homework-level rotation-matrix question, and is dense_low_card_high -- suggesting the scorecard rewards visible machinery even when it overshoots what the question calls for.

selected.name: Self-contained completion
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the answer reaches the requested conclusion with all essential definitions and steps included; score 0 when it is only a hint, approval, citation, or fragment that requires substantial reconstruction.
selected.rationale: R10 and R11 provide partial computational guidance, while R16, R26, and R32 are especially dependent on the reader supplying missing work.
member_names: Closes the loop, or makes the remainder explicitly mechanical

selected.name: Decisive counterexample construction
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the answer gives a simple counterexample, verifies the relevant hypothesis, and demonstrates the failure; score 0 when it merely asserts falsity or gives an unverified example.
selected.rationale: R01, R24, R38, and R55 use concrete counterexamples or reductions to expose false universal claims.
member_names: Example or counterexample that is actually verified
Refutation carried through to a repair

selected.name: Cross-Method Verification
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the answer confirms its result through two or more genuinely independent mathematical methods or perspectives. Score 0 if only one method or path is used, or if the 'second method' is merely a restatement of the first.
selected.rationale: R15 derives the recursion formula for the nth derivative and then independently confirms via Taylor expansion, giving the asker two ways to see the answer. R52 confirms via rank arguments and then offers SVD as an alternative perspective. The dense model credits this redundancy as confidence-building; the scorecard may see it as unnecessary.

selected.name: Notational Discipline and Consistency
selected.instruction: Score 10 if mathematical notation is clean, standard, consistent throughout, and well-formatted. Score 0 if notation is confusing, inconsistent, non-standard, or acknowledged as broken.
selected.rationale: R38 uses clean aligned equations with a color-coded correction; R39 uses clear recursive notation with explicit definitions. The dense model rewards both. R22 uses informal abbreviations ('U have') and R47 explicitly asks 'can somebody please fix up my TeX,' signaling notational problems the dense model apparently detects.

selected.name: Generalizable method extraction
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the answer clearly identifies a reusable strategy and demonstrates why it works; score 0 when it gives only an isolated calculation with no transferable method.
selected.rationale: R18, R23, R39, and R47 expose recurring techniques involving recurrences, roots of unity, modular reduction, or cycle powers.

selected.name: Insight density relative to length
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on the ratio of genuine mathematical insight to verbiage. 10 = a short answer that delivers the key trick/observation with almost no throat-clearing or restatement (high insight per line). 0 = long exposition padded with restated setup, redundant notation-juggling, or repeated intermediate steps that add length without new insight.
selected.rationale: R07 (three sentences: 123 and 321 are both multiples of 3, so the sum can't be 1 mod 3) and R55 (a two-line algebraic identity answer) are terse and high-insight; contrast the much longer, step-padded R10 and R56, which are dense_low_card_high despite (or because of) their length.
member_names: Insight density: distinct ideas per unit of length

selected.name: Invites reader dialogue or explicitly requests feedback
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer directly addresses the reader with a question or request (e.g., asking if the explanation makes sense, or asking for help/correction from others). 10 = the answer ends with or contains an explicit question/request directed at the reader/community. 0 = the answer is a pure monologue with no direct address inviting a response.
selected.rationale: R33 closes with 'Does that make sense?' and R25 closes with 'can somebody please fix up my TeX so the chunk equations is centred and aligned?' -- both open a dialogue with the reader rather than delivering a closed monologue, and both are dense_high_card_low.
member_names: Explicit engagement with other answers/answerers on the thread

selected.name: Intuition tied to formal meaning
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an accessible analogy or geometric interpretation is explicitly linked to the relevant definition or formula; score 0 when the analogy is vague, misleading, or never connected back to mathematics.
selected.rationale: R16 connects entropy to expected code length and then states the mathematical bound; R15 explains sampling density through grid counts and the relation N=k^p.

selected.name: Domain and exception discipline
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the answer explicitly tracks domains, denominators, convergence regions, endpoints, or branch restrictions and adjusts its claims accordingly; score 0 when it silently treats a restricted statement as globally valid.
selected.rationale: R14, R19, R20, R23, R49, and R54 each hinge on restrictions that must be stated or checked.

selected.name: Names a canonical object as a load-bearing shortcut, not as trivia
selected.instruction: When the answer invokes a named theorem or named object, score whether the name does work. 10 = naming it immediately settles or reorganizes the question (invoking the theorem is the answer, or the isomorphism to a known classified object reduces the problem to lookup). 5 = the name is correct and relevant but the answer would be unchanged without it. 0 = the name is decorative -- supplied as interesting background alongside a derivation that never uses it -- or no naming occurs where one would obviously help.
selected.rationale: R11 (dense .941 / card .260) opens by observing the hypotheses violate Clairaut's theorem, which settles the question outright; R21 (dense .764 / card .150) is one line, G/Z(G) = Inn(G), which converts the exercise into a lookup; R42 (dense .820 / card .212) reduces the problem to the known subgroup lattice of D_6. Against these, R40 (dense .379 / card .924) names the director circle 'for the sake of interest' and then grinds through Vieta anyway, and R10 (dense .116 / card .739) names the order-statistics family as an aside. Same surface feature -- a correct technical name -- pulling opposite ways, which is exactly the kind of distinction a flat criterion would blur.
member_names: Names a canonical object as a load-bearing shortcut, not as trivia
Names a result that immediately settles the question

selected.name: Hint hands back a specific next action rather than a formula
selected.instruction: For answers that deliberately withhold the full solution, score whether the withholding is constructive. 10 = the answer stages the remaining work as named steps or a pointed question the asker can act on immediately ('show X; then show Y; then apply both twice'; 'which terms survive at x=0?'), so the asker knows exactly what to do next. 5 = a relevant fact or substitution is offered but the asker must guess how it connects to their problem. 0 = a bare formula, expression, or assertion is dropped with the label 'hint' and no route from it to the goal. Answers that give the complete solution are scored on whether an equivalent next-step structure is present in the exposition; a complete, well-staged solution can score high.
selected.rationale: R19 (dense .952 / card .344) is nothing but a three-rung ladder ending in 'apply (1) and (2) twice'; R43 (dense .845 / card .165) shows the expansion and then asks the asker which terms matter at x=0. Both are card-low. Compare R51 (dense .076 / card .631), a 'hint' that is a closed-form infinite sum with no indication of how to evaluate it, and R52's card score (.113) versus its dense .850 despite being a chain of substitutions. The scorecard appears to penalize incompleteness uniformly; the dense model seems to distinguish scaffolding from abandonment.
member_names: Hint hands back a specific next action rather than a formula
Socratic hint that leaves the final step to the reader

selected.name: Structure-revealing transformation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a substitution, factorization, invariant, or change of representation makes the underlying structure evident and is explained; score 0 when algebraic transformations remain opaque or merely procedural.
selected.rationale: R01 uses sheet and argument structure, R18 uses a derivative recurrence, R23 uses roots of unity, and R60 rewrites inequalities into tractable auxiliary functions.

selected.name: Sustained second-person address to this asker
selected.instruction: Score how consistently the answer is written to the person who asked, using the text alone. 10 = second-person address runs through the answer, the asker's own notation and framing are adopted, and the answer checks comprehension or anticipates the asker's next confusion. 5 = occasional 'you' inside an otherwise impersonal exposition. 0 = fully impersonal exposition in the answer's own notation, indistinguishable from a textbook passage on the topic.
selected.rationale: R04 (dense .945 / card .229) reads the asker's own stem-and-leaf rows back to them and ends 'Does that make sense?'; R55 says 'you seem to be greatly confused' and then 'let me dispel that confusion'; R38 (dense .784 / card .177) walks the asker through their own expression and ends 'hopefully this shows...'. Opposite pole: R50 (dense .282 / card .998, the highest card score in the slice) is a polished impersonal essay on entropy addressed to no one in particular, and R18 (dense .095 / card .932) is a generic grid explanation. Register is exactly the kind of property an explicit-criterion bank tends to omit as non-mathematical.
member_names: Sustained second-person address to this asker
Written to this asker rather than to a general reader

selected.name: Transparent Limitation Acknowledgment
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the answer openly acknowledges that its own method is incomplete, that something is broken, or that the approach has limitations—while still being useful. Score 0 if the answer presents itself as complete and authoritative without acknowledging any gaps or issues.
selected.rationale: R09 provides a computation and then immediately flags 'this is broken,' which signals intellectual honesty that voters trust. R10 includes a candid editorial opinion ('there's basically no reason to use them anymore... kind of silly') that signals the answerer's expertise. The scorecard may penalize such admissions rather than crediting the transparency.

selected.name: Post-hoc edit/revision marker
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the text contains explicit revision markers such as 'EDIT:', 'Edit:', 'P.S.', or language flagging that material was added or corrected after the original post (e.g. 'I have three suggestions', 'this is broken'). Score only the extent of these revision markers, not whether the edit made the answer better or worse.
selected.rationale: R35 ('EDIT: I have three suggestions...') and R45 ('edit: And well, this is broken.') both carry visible post-hoc revision markers absent from single-pass answers like R23 or R32; an editing history is an upstream production-process trace that could also indicate a genuinely more carefully corrected final answer.
member_names: Post-hoc maintenance marks and meta-commentary about the post
Visible revision trace and appended afterthoughts

selected.name: Dense structured mathematical display
selected.instruction: Score the extent of heavy structured mathematical formatting: multi-line aligned environments, large matrices, numbered/tagged equations, multi-row derivations using begin/end environments, and systematic display-mode typesetting. 0 = only inline or simple math, 10 = answer is dominated by complex display structures. Do NOT judge whether the formatting is good.
selected.rationale: Heavy display formatting may impress a scorecard (looks thorough) but is a habit, not a quality signal. R10 uses a large inverse-matrix display; R09 features a multi-row argument matrix and detailed multi-part derivation; R48 has aligned multi-line derivations -- all dense-low-card-high.

selected.name: Orthographic slips and informal typing hygiene
selected.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT of surface language-production slips: chat-style abbreviations of ordinary words (single-letter 'U' for 'you', 'cause' for 'because'), missing spaces after sentence-final or list punctuation, spaces placed before commas, misspellings of ordinary or technical English words, non-standard comparative or plural forms, dropped function words that make a phrase ungrammatical, unmatched or improvised quotation marks around ordinary terms, and run-on sentences with commas doing the work of periods. 0 = clean, conventionally edited English; 10 = slips of these kinds in most sentences. Do NOT count mathematical errors, and do NOT count deliberate informality that is otherwise correctly written. You MUST NOT judge whether the writing is good, professional, or easy to read; score only the density of these surface slips.
selected.rationale: A typing-hygiene trace that a text model can read off directly while it says nothing about within-question crowd preference on its own. R10 writes 'U have', 'U want', 'Simplier', 'chosing'; R17 writes 'You mixed them up.If you look at' and ',firstly at'; R12 writes 'switchs' and long comma-spliced sentences; R03 writes 'independant'; R34 writes 'I leave it you to simplify'. Tagged mixed because hurried or non-native composition may co-occur with genuinely less careful mathematics.
member_names: Informal or non-LaTeX mathematical notation in text

selected.name: Diagnosing the asker's posted attempt versus standalone exposition
selected.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the answer is addressed to one particular person's already-posted work rather than written as a self-contained exposition for a general reader. Traces to count: second-person verdicts on that person's attempt ('you did it correctly', 'that looks fine to me', 'you are correct except', 'you mixed them up', 'you seem to be confused'); quotation of the asker's own lines or symbols back at them; localisation of a specific slip to a specific step or sign; instructions phrased as what 'you' should do next with 'your' expression; conversational check-ins directed at that person. Score LOW when the text never presumes any prior attempt and reads as an exposition a stranger could land on cold. 0 = fully standalone exposition; 10 = line-by-line correction of one person's posted work throughout. You MUST NOT judge whether personal, corrective engagement is helpful or whether standalone exposition is better; score only which mode of address is present and how strongly.
selected.rationale: This distinguishes two writing stances that are driven by the thread situation, not by mathematical merit. R57 opens 'You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end'; R35 opens 'You are correct except one sign'; R41 opens 'That looks fine to me'; R06 opens 'Your DFA looks good to me'; R09, R44 and R53 all diagnose the asker's own construction. At the other pole R15 and R20 are self-contained expositions addressed to no one in particular, and R50 explains a general trick. Tagged mixed because a well-aimed diagnosis of the asker's specific error can be genuinely what the thread needed.

selected.name: Explicit cross-reference to other answers or comments
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer text explicitly references, quotes, defers to, corrects, or builds on another specific answer or comment on the same page (e.g. 'as was pointed out in another answer', 'to expand on Stephen's answer', 'I see I've just repeated X's comment'). Do NOT judge whether referencing others is good; score only how much explicit cross-referencing is present.
selected.rationale: These fingerprints reveal the answer is NOT the first to arrive. R16 ('As was pointed out in another answer'), R26 (quoting Ove Ahlman's answer), R34 ('As in my post'), R38 ('nicely considered in the answer from @ErickWong'), R49 ('To expand on Stephen's answer'), and R59 ('I see I've just repeated Daniel Schepler's comment here') all leak arrival order. First answers cannot reference others, so this channel is a direct position proxy that the dense model may treat as 'derivative' and the card model may miss.

selected.name: Hint-mode withholding versus delivered completion
selected.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the answer deliberately stops short and hands the remaining work back to the reader. Traces to count: an explicit hint label opening the post, in any casing; a numbered programme of things the reader is told to 'show' or 'prove' themselves; explicit statements that the remainder is left to the reader or that the reader should now simplify, finish, or figure out what happens next; a closing question put back to the reader; a final line that names the next step without taking it. Score LOW when the argument is carried all the way to a stated conclusion or final value. 0 = complete worked argument ending in its conclusion; 10 = nothing but a pointer or opening move with the work explicitly delegated. You MUST NOT judge whether hinting is pedagogically right or whether a full solution is better; score only how much of the work is withheld.
selected.rationale: Hint-mode is a house style acquired from the venue, and it is orthogonal to whether the mathematics behind it is sound. R29 opens 'HINT: Work up to it in steps:' and lists three things for the reader to show; R07, R39, R42, R43 and R59 all open with a hint label; R23 opens 'Hint:' and then points elsewhere; R34 closes 'I leave it you to simplify this expression'; R22 closes 'Now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic'; R26 closes 'Does that make sense?'. Contrast R31 and R14, which carry a full argument to its contradiction. Tagged mixed because a practised answerer's judgement about how much to withhold may itself track what the thread wanted.
member_names: Hint mode: deliberate withholding of the completed solution

selected.name: Meta-commentary and self-referential asides
selected.instruction: Score the extent of meta-textual commentary: P.S. notes, 'Hope this helps!', edit annotations, formatting requests directed at other users, parenthetical notes explaining the answer itself, and asides about the answering process. 0 = none, 10 = pervasive. Do NOT judge whether these are helpful.
selected.rationale: Meta-commentary is pure surface noise that a scorecard may read as thoroughness. R06 has a P.S. explaining why computations were added; R17 ends 'Hope this helps!' with an EDIT note; R48 asks 'can somebody please fix up my TeX'; R56 has two signed notes -- all dense-low-card-high.

selected.name: Boilerplate scaffolding
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the presence and repetition of stock instructional phrases or templates such as 'Hint', 'Let', 'It is clear', 'You are correct', or 'For example'; do not judge whether the template is helpful.
selected.rationale: Canned phrasing may be predictive as a stylistic fingerprint while carrying no direct information about mathematical merit. R03 begins with 'Hint', and R07 uses a standard correction template followed by staged algebra.
